lead: A classifier turns labelled feature vectors into a rule that names a new vector's class. It does this by placing a decision boundary in feature space: minimum distance uses class means, k-nearest neighbour uses nearby stored samples, and Bayes uses probability densities and priors. These are the classical recognition rules used on small or medium feature sets such as colour histograms or short HOG summaries, and they still serve as baselines when a deep model is too heavy. This chapter shows how each rule draws its boundary and how the three relate.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for feature vectors and pattern classes.

blocks.text: Class ω_j has N_j labelled training vectors. Its prototype is the class mean: m_j = (1/N_j) Σ x, summed over the N_j samples in ω_j. A test vector x goes to the class whose prototype is nearest. The rule uses squared Euclidean distance. Expanding it gives the formula below; xᵀx is the same for every class, so it cannot change the ranking. The remaining score g_j(x) = m_jᵀx − ½m_jᵀm_j is a linear discriminant. Assign x to the class with the largest g_j. Between two classes the boundary g_i = g_j is a straight line, a hyperplane in higher dimensions. For two classes it is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining m₁ and m₂. In the figure m₁=(0,2), m₂=(4,2), x=(1.2,2): d₁=1.2, d₂=2.8, so x→ω₁. This rule assumes each class is a compact cloud around its mean. A long or unevenly spread class breaks that assumption.

blocks.where: d_j² is the squared distance to class j; x is the test vector; m_j is the prototype of class j; ᵀ marks transpose; ‖·‖ is Euclidean length.
g_j is the linear discriminant for class j; the class with the largest g_j is chosen.

blocks.text: k-NN stores all labelled training vectors. For test x, compute distance to every stored vector, keep the k smallest, and take a majority vote of their labels. k=1 is the nearest neighbour rule: copy the label of the closest sample. For two classes use odd k so a tie cannot occur. Euclidean distance is usual; Manhattan distance is the sum of the absolute coordinate differences, Σ|xᵢ − yᵢ|, and is an option. Feature scaling is not optional. If one feature ranges over thousands and another over 0 to 1, the large-range feature controls every distance. Standardise each feature to zero mean and unit variance, or map it to [0,1], before k-NN. Training cost is only storage, O(Nd) for N vectors in d dimensions. Test cost is O(Nd), because no compact model is built. A large training set gives accuracy but slow prediction. Speed-ups index the vectors, for example with a k-d tree or approximate nearest neighbour search.

Bayes decision uses probabilities. Let P(ω_j) be the prior probability of class j, p(x|ω_j) the class-conditional density of x, and p(x) the evidence. The posterior is P(ω_j|x) = p(x|ω_j)P(ω_j)/p(x). With 0-1 loss, which charges 0 for a correct label and 1 for an error, choose the class with the largest posterior; this minimises the probability of error. The same choice maximises g_j(x)=ln p(x|ω_j)+ln P(ω_j), because p(x) is common. The Bayes error rate is the unavoidable error of this rule; it depends on how much the class densities overlap. For two classes a confusion matrix counts true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives on test data. For J classes it is a J×J table, and these four counts are read off one class at a time. It reports what the rule did, not the theoretical minimum. For Gaussian classes with equal, isotropic covariance Σ = σ²I and equal priors, the Bayes boundary is exactly the minimum distance boundary: the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the means. With equal but general Σ the Bayes rule still has a linear boundary, but it uses the squared Mahalanobis distance (x−m_j)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x−m_j); that boundary is a straight line, not in general the perpendicular bisector. Unequal priors move the boundary toward the less likely class: a rare class needs stronger evidence. Unequal covariance matrices give a curved, quadratic boundary.

blocks.where: P(ω_j|x) is the posterior of class j; p(x|ω_j) is the class-conditional density; P(ω_j) is the prior; p(x) is the evidence.
g_j is the Bayes discriminant; ln is natural logarithm; the largest g_j gives the minimum-error decision.

figure.caption: Class means from the worked example are m₁ = (2, 2.67) and m₂ = (6, 4.67); the test point x = (4, 3) is 2.03 from m₁ and 2.60 from m₂, so it lies on the ω₁ side of the perpendicular bisector and the rule labels it ω₁. With equal priors and equal isotropic covariance σ²I this same line is the Bayes boundary.

spec.aria: Two class means in a two-dimensional feature space, a test point closer to the first mean, and the straight perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the means separating the two sides.

examples.question: Training samples: ω₁ = (1,2), (2,3), (3,3); ω₂ = (5,4), (6,5), (7,5). Test vector x = (4,3). (a) Apply the minimum distance classifier. (b) Apply 3-NN.
steps: d₁ < d₂, so minimum distance gives ω₁.
The three nearest are (3,3) at 1.0000 (ω₁), (5,4) at 1.4142 (ω₂), and (2,3) at 2.0000 (ω₁). Votes: 2 for ω₁, 1 for ω₂.
examples.answer: Both rules assign x=(4,3) to class ω₁; minimum distance uses d₁=2.0276 < d₂=2.6034 and 3-NN votes 2:1.
examples.check:
import math
w1=[(1,2),(2,3),(3,3)]
w2=[(5,4),(6,5),(7,5)]
x=(4,3)
m1=(sum(p[0] for p in w1)/len(w1), sum(p[1] for p in w1)/len(w1))
m2=(sum(p[0] for p in w2)/len(w2), sum(p[1] for p in w2)/len(w2))
d1sq=(x[0]-m1[0])**2+(x[1]-m1[1])**2
d2sq=(x[0]-m2[0])**2+(x[1]-m2[1])**2
d1=math.sqrt(d1sq)
d2=math.sqrt(d2sq)
print(round(m1[0],4))
print(round(m1[1],4))
print(round(m2[0],4))
print(round(m2[1],4))
print(round(d1sq,4))
print(round(d1,4))
print(round(d2sq,4))
print(round(d2,4))
pts=[(p,1) for p in w1]+[(p,2) for p in w2]
for p,lab in pts:
    print(round(math.dist(x,p),4))
pts.sort(key=lambda q: math.dist(x,q[0]))
top=pts[:3]
v1=sum(1 for _,lab in top if lab==1)
v2=sum(1 for _,lab in top if lab==2)
print(v1)
print(v2)

traps: Unscaled features let a large-range feature dominate k-NN; standardise first.
An even k can tie with two classes; use odd k unless a tie rule is given.

Minimum distance is not Bayes in general; it is Bayes only for Gaussian classes with equal isotropic covariance σ²I and equal priors. With equal but general covariance the Bayes rule is nearest mean in Mahalanobis distance, and the boundary is a straight line but not the perpendicular bisector.
The prototype is the class mean, not the nearest training sample; k=1 uses the sample.
Bayes error is the theoretical minimum; a confusion matrix is measured test performance, not the same number.

quiz.q: Define the prototype m_j in the minimum distance classifier.
quiz.a: The mean vector of the training samples in class ω_j: m_j=(1/N_j)Σx.

quiz.q: Why can xᵀx be dropped from d_j² when comparing classes?
quiz.a: It is identical for every class, so it changes all scores equally and cannot change the largest g_j.

quiz.q: m₁=(0,0), m₂=(6,0). Classify x=(2,1) by minimum distance.
In 5-NN the five nearest labels are ω₁, ω₂, ω₂, ω₁, ω₂. What is the decision?
Why use odd k for two classes?
How do unequal priors change a Bayes boundary between two Gaussian classes with equal covariance?
quiz.a: The boundary shifts toward the class with smaller prior; the more likely class needs less evidence. With equal priors and equal isotropic covariance σ²I it is the minimum distance line (the perpendicular bisector). With equal but general covariance the boundary is linear but uses Mahalanobis distance, not Euclidean minimum distance.

quiz.q: Give one reason k-NN is slow at test time and one fix.
quiz.a: It compares x with all N stored vectors, O(Nd); use an index such as a k-d tree or approximate nearest neighbour search.

quiz.q: What is the Bayes error rate?
quiz.a: The minimum probability of error of the Bayes rule, set by class overlap.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice these classifiers run after a feature extractor, for example HOG for pedestrians or colour histograms for a phone photo tagger. k-NN at scale becomes approximate nearest neighbour search, used inside image retrieval and face matching. Bayes ideas reappear in probabilistic classifiers and in the softmax layer of a CNN, which is trained as a conditional probability model. Search terms: scikit-learn KNeighborsClassifier, FAISS, nearest neighbour search, linear discriminant analysis.
